title: Do Not Draft by Predicted Injuries, Except Chronic Cases
brief: Why are games played and injury-prone labels poor predictors, and which cases (repeated same-spot lower-body injuries, big men with foot problems, degenerative injuries) should still lower a player's price? It must also cover not stacking several risky players and why injury risk costs more in head-to-head than in roto.
summary: Games played barely repeats from one season to the next, so do not pay extra for "iron men" and do not cut a player's price just because he has an "injury-prone" label. Lower your bid only for chronic cases: repeated injuries or surgeries to the same lower-body spot, big men with foot problems, and degenerative injuries. Then limit yourself to one such player per roster, because in 9-cat head-to-head a missed week costs you more than it would in roto.

sections.heading: Why games played and labels mislead

paragraphs.text: Games played from one season to the next has a correlation of only about 0.3. Using two years of history only raises it to 0.35. Among the top 250 players by minutes it drops to 0.2. That is too weak to price. Totals rankings and labels like "injury prone" or "iron man" carry little signal.

Injuries are largely unpredictable. A player seen as fragile can stay healthy, and a durable player can get hurt. Being healthy last season says little about this season. Drafting a player because you expect him not to get hurt does not work.

Availability alone has no value. Many low-value players played 82 games. If a player's per-game line would not make one of our 144 rosters, playing every game does not change that. Do not bid more on a player just because he played a full season.

Avoid one-year blindness. The consensus often calls a player injury prone or healthy after one season. That label is weak evidence, but it moves auction prices. Expect the room to overreact, and do not let one season flip a long-term view.

sections.heading: Check the context behind missed games

paragraphs.text: Before you lower a bid, find out why the games were missed. Games sat out while a team was tanking do not show injury risk. On a team out of contention, minor injuries can look worse than they are. On a good team, the same player might play through them.
A games-played total can also overstate how healthy a player really was. Many of Jalen Williams' 40 games came on limited minutes while he recovered. Check minutes, not just games.

Some context supports availability. A player close to a contract extension has a reason to reach the 65-game threshold. A back problem that recurred during a season can improve with a full offseason of rest. Worry again only if it flares up in training camp, which you can check before our 2026-10-18 auction.

Short-term injuries at the start of the season deserve some caution. But the season is 25 weeks long, so do not drop the price too far. One exception: hamstring injuries tend to come back. A long early ruling on a hamstring can mean the team is being careful, or that the injury is serious.

sections.heading: The chronic cases that should lower a price

paragraphs.text: Lower your bid when a player has repeated injuries or surgeries to the same lower-body part, especially the knees, or an ongoing mystery illness. Problems that keep returning to the same spot make future missed time more likely. Bid below his per-game value. Hand, finger, shoulder and oblique injuries matter little. Concussions matter a little.

Big men with foot problems are the clearest case. Very large players with repeated foot and ankle problems are a risky mix. Foot injuries can change the path of a seven-footer's career. Big men jump, contest and land on bodies, so a slow recovery can push them past opening night. Their repeated lower-body problems rarely go away.

A degenerative injury stays priced in even after a healthy year. One good season does not remove the risk. Injuries caused by a player's own all-out style are also more likely to return than random contact injuries.

The cost can last longer than the missed games. Some players lose production for a long time after even a minor injury. For these chronic cases, one expert drops the player a tier or more and will not take Kawhi Leonard before pick 40. In our 12-team league, pick 40 is around each team's fourth player. Treat a chronic case as a mid-roster buy, not a core purchase.

As a general rule, do not roster several players you have injury worries about. Pairing two injury-risk stars, such as Anthony Davis and Kawhi Leonard, on one team is very risky. This holds even when each one looks like good value at his price. Be extra careful with old players who have repeated lower-body injuries early in the draft.

Before you raise your bid on a risky player, count the big risks already on your roster. Take a high-risk player late only if you have not already bought anything very risky earlier. A practical rule for our 12-man rosters: one chronic case at most, and none if your early buys already carry health questions.
Injury risk also works the other way. If a teammate is injury prone, his missed games can open up usage for your player. Factor that in when you weigh a risky teammate pair.

sections.heading: Why risk costs more in head-to-head

paragraphs.text: Several experts agree that injuries matter less in roto than in head-to-head. Injury-prone stars like Kawhi Leonard and Joel Embiid worked in roto. In head-to-head they should be pushed down. In roto, a missed stretch is spread over a full season of totals. In our league, each week is its own matchup across 9 categories.

A player who plays only about two games in a week can lose you categories even when his per-game line is strong. In a deep league, a missed game means a much worse replacement has to start. With 144 players drafted and a limit of 6 acquisitions per week, our waiver wire cannot fully cover a missing star. Limited streaming is exactly when experts say to avoid players who miss games often.

Availability is the biggest threat to a top player's value. In one review, 54% of exits from the top 25 came from injury-shortened seasons, not from worse play. Our playoffs are weeks 19 to 21 and end 2027-03-28. A chronic case who goes down in March can cost you a playoff matchup.

The experts split on how much discount the market already applies. One side says to push risky players down a tier or more and warns against being comfortable with injury risk. The other side says drafters are too scared of players returning from last season's injuries. On this view, the market overprices risk for some veterans. If your valuation holds while public opinion drops, you get value. A health-risk player like Kristaps Porzingis is worth a late-middle-round pick. One expert adds that the new IL rule, which lets injured players go on IL as soon as they are ruled out, may mean injury-prone players should not drop further. We have 4 IL slots. Against this, another expert warns that an injury-prone player taken around pick 110 in a deep league is a big risk. Our approach: let the room push these players down, then bid only when the price is clearly below your per-game value and you hold no other big risk.
